history: A Brief History of Saugus High Football
Introduction

Saugus High School’s football program boasts over a century of tradition marked by unforgettable triumphs, legendary players, and the unyielding spirit of a small-town community in Massachusetts. From its humble beginnings in the early 1900s to its golden era of state championships, the Sachems have woven a rich tapestry of history that continues to inspire “Sachem Pride” to this day. This overview traces the program’s key eras, coaches, stars, and milestones, celebrating its enduring legacy despite recent challenges.
1900–1919 (The Early Years):
J.W. Stanley (1901)

The earliest Saugus High football team was the 1901 team, coached by J.W. Stanley and was led by player Chas Bennett. There wasn’t much recorded during these earlier years, and it appears that Saugus High went on to have a long stretch with little or no organized football before the program became more consistent in the 1910s.
Arthur L. William (1914)

Saugus High has fielded a football team in most seasons since 1914. The 1914 team was coached by Arthur L. William. Saugus went 2-7 during Coach Williams’ lone season as Head Coach. The team was led by players John Fox and George Sprague.
Charles T. Senay (1915-1916)

Charles T. Senay took over as Head Coach for the 1915 and 1916 seasons and led Saugus to a respectable 6-0 and 7-1 record. The team was led by notable players like Sprague, John Flynn, and Mike Garofano, who is often remembered as the program’s first star player. Garofano would miss his senior season to fight in World War I for the United States.
Edward Collier (1917-1918)
Edward Collier took over in 1917 and led the team to a 0-5 record. The season was cut short and there was no 1918 season found on record. This was most likely due to the Spanish Flu pandemic.
1920–1950: (The Golden Years):

The period from 1920 through 1950 is widely regarded as the “Golden Era” of Saugus football. During that stretch, Saugus won state championships in 1941 and 1944 and Exchange Bowl championships in 1949 and 1950, and produced several other teams that were strong enough to be considered among the best in program history.
Fred Beresford (1920–1922, 1928)

Fred Beresford arrived in 1920 and helped build Saugus into a highly competitive team. His 1922 squad went 9-0-2 and was one of the earliest great Saugus teams. Whether that team was officially recognized as a state champion is disputed, but it was clearly one of the strongest in the school’s early history. The 1922 team was led by players Franklin "Ooze" Pike, John Pike, Forrest Kenerson, Podge Herold, Lester Pool, and Googie Emery.
William Bangs (1923–1925)

William Bangs took over in 1923 and coached through 1925. Bangs maintained competitiveness but did not produce a winning season, finishing 6–6 in his final year. Some notable players on those Bangs teams were Pool and Emery, as well as Ernest Belliveau, Homer McNutt, Wally Guatreau, and Danton Sawyer.

Albion Rice was hired in 1926 and would help stabilize the program through 1934, with Fred Beresford briefly returning in 1928 (a disappointing 0-9 season) before Rice came back the next season. During his tenure Saugus had some success. Rice’s best team was his 1931 team that went 7-2. That team was led by George Riley, Joe Nelson, Malcolm Bisbee, Harry Gates, Red Doherty, and Joe Scarozza. There were other notable players during the Coach Rice era such as Forrest Rhodes, Jack Leahy, Wally Guatreau, John H. Pike, Arthur Martin, Stuart Kidder, Reggie Goss, Gilman Cann, Vincent Pendleton, Dizzy Pierce, Joseph Pendleton, Burton Norton, Alec Ozahowski, and Gerard Brazis, Phillip Hallam, Warren Vatcher, and Burton Norton.
John “Jack” Leahy (1935–1936)

John “Jack” Leahy took over the Sachems for the 1935 and 1936 seasons. Saugus had a very good 1935 season going 6-3. Some notable players from that 1935 team were Gerard Brazis, Phillip Hallam, Warren Vatcher, and Burton Norton. The 1936 Saugus team however dropped to 2-7-1.

Throughout its history, Saugus has primarily been known as the Sachems, a nickname that began during the Leahy era. Prior to the Sachems nickname and mascot, Saugus used other nicknames including Warriors (1914–1929) and Eagles (1930–1934).
Charles “Buzz” Harvey (1937–1940)

Saugus hired Charles “Buzz” Harvey in 1937, a 1934 graduate of Holy Cross, where he was a 1933 Football All-American and a member of the Holy Cross Athletic Hall Of Fame, to take over for Leahy. Harvey coached Saugus until 1940. Harvey saw great success during his 4-year tenure. Harvey coached some of the best football players to ever play for Saugus. These players include Jim Fauci (His son, John, would go on to become the Sachems Head Coach in 1996), Bud McKay, George Flaherty, and legendary players Art Statuto and John “Iron Mike” Harrington, both who would play a huge part on the 1941 Saugus State Championship team. Stan Green was also another legend from the 1939 team. He was named to the Boston Herald and Boston Post All Scholastic team and would go on to play college football at Columbia. Coach Harvey would step down as head coach of Saugus after the 1940 season and would go on to become coach at Nashua High School in New Hampshire, where he would lead that program to over 200 wins and 11 state championships, becoming one of the State of New Hampshire’s greatest High School Football Coaches.
Henry “Hammering Hank” Toczylowski (1941–1942)

Coach Harvey was succeeded by Henry “Hammering Hank” Toczylowski, a rising football star who had been drafted by the NFL’s Brooklyn Dodgers in 1941. Despite the opportunity to pursue a professional career, Toczylowski chose instead to coach and teach at Saugus High School. At the time of his hiring, he was a recent graduate of Boston College. In his senior season at Boston College in 1940, Toczylowski served as starting quarterback and team captain of the undefeated “Team of Destiny,” which finished 11–0. The Eagles recorded six shutouts and capped their season with a victory in the Sugar Bowl. He played under legendary coach Frank Leahy, who later won multiple national championships at Notre Dame (1943, 1946–47, 1949). Toczylowski was also named a First-Team All-American that season.

In his first year as head coach at Saugus in 1941, Toczylowski led the Sachems to a 10–0–1 record and the program’s first state championship (Class C). The team featured several standout players previously coached by Harvey, including Statuto and Harrington, as well as Art McDonald, Eddie “Shipper” Shipulski, and Eddie Koschei. Harrington was a 2-time Football Captain for the Sachems. He was named to the Boston Herald, Boston Globe, WESX, and North Shore All Scholastic team his senior season. He also excelled as a baseball player. Unfortunately, his athletic career was cut short after his senior year due to an accident. Statuto went on to become a 3-time National Champion at Notre Dame (1943, 1946-1947) and played professionally for the Buffalo Bills in All American Football Conference and the Los Angeles Rams of the NFL. Toczylowski followed up with a 7–3–1 season in 1942 before stepping down to serve in World War II. He is a member of the Massachusetts High School Football Coaches Association Hall of Fame.
Dave Lucey (1943–1946)

Dave Lucey, another former member of the undefeated 1940 Boston College Eagles Football team and was a back up to Coach Toczylowski on that team, was hired to replace Coach Toczylowski in 1943 and would coach the Sachems through 1946. Coach Lucey guided Saugus to its greatest season, a 10-0 championship run in 1944. During the 1944 Championship season, Saugus scored 207 points while only allowing 19. The 1944 team had many great players such as Art Spinney, Dick Allen, Bob Kane, Don Reiniger, Doug Waybright, and Frank Pyzsko. Pyzsko was named Boston Globe and Post All Scholastic. Art Spinney, one of the greatest football players to ever come of Massachusetts, was named to several All-State teams; In 2024 he would be named to the Boston Globes All-Time All-Scholastic Football Team. Spinney would go on to play collegiately at Boston College where he was a four-year starter and named captain during his senior season. Spinney would be inducted into the Boston College Athletic Hall of Fame in 1972. After college, Spinney was drafted by Baltimore Colts of the NFL in 1950, however he only played in two games during his rookie season before he would be drafted into Army to fight in the Korean War. Spinney would miss the rest of the 1950 season and all of the 1951 and 1952 season due to his military service. In 1953 Spinney signed with the Cleveland Browns as a free agent, however he would be traded to the Baltimore Colts before the season. The Colts were an expansion team in 1953 as the 1950 Baltimore Colts Franchise had folded after the 1950 season. Spinney would play for the Colts from 1953 through 1960. Spinney was a 3-time All Pro (1958-1960), 2-time Pro Bowler (1959-1960) and 2-time NFL Champion (1958-1959). Some of Spinney’s teammates during his seasons with the Colts were Pro Football Hall of Famers Raymond Berry, Art Donovan, Gino Marchetti, Lenny Moore, Jim Parker, Johnn Unitas, and Don Shula. Spinney would retire from the NFL in 1960. Doug Waybright was another legend from the Lucey era. Waybright went on to play College Football at Notre Dame (1944, 1947-1949). He was a member of the 1947 and 1949 National Championship teams (along with former Sachem teammate Art Statuto) while playing for Notre Dame. After college he served in the military before he returned to Saugus, where he was very active in youth sports. He was so beloved by the town that when he passed away at the young age of 38, officials named an elementary school in his honor.
1947–1960: (The Janusas Era):
Jon Janusas (1947–1960)

Jon Janusas took over in 1947 and is generally regarded as one of the most successful coaches in Saugus and Massachusetts High School Football history, as he is a member of both the Saugus High School Athletic Hall of Fame and Massachusetts High School Football Coaches Association Hall of Fame. He is also a member of the Boston College Athletic Hall of Fame as a player (Boston College Graduate, 1938). His Sachem teams won Exchange Bowl championships (a bowl game held in Massachusetts by the Exchange Club of Lynn) in 1949 and 1950, giving Saugus back-to-back title seasons at the end of the “Golden Era”. The 1950 team was the last school to win the Exchange Bowl and with it the trophy that is proudly retired to the high school awards display case. The back-to-back Exchange Bowl championships were probably the program’s greatest accomplishment.

The 1947 Sachems went 7-3 and were led by Ernie Anganis, Sardi Nicolo, Eugene Decereau, and George Lasky. Lasky was the star of that 1947 team. Lasky won numerous awards through his High School career including the Sgt. Arthur Defranzo Player of the Year Award in 1946 and 1947, the Thomas Atkins Memorial Award in 1946, and was named to the Boston Globe, Boston Post, Lynn Item, and North Shore All Scholastic teams in 1947. The 1948 Sachems team had an off year going a disappointing 3-8.

The 1949 Sachems went 10-1, winning the Exchange Bowl against Weymouth 7-6. This game will forever be remembered for the last second 50-yard Touchdown pass QB Richie Nicolo threw to his older brother, Sal ‘Sardi’, for the game tying score followed by the game winning extra point made by Jimmy Kane. The 1949 squad scored 230 Points on the season while only allowing 41 points. They went on to shut out 5 teams (consecutively) during the season. Their lone loss was a 20-15 loss to the Beverly Panthers. That 1949 team was led by Dan Murphy, Fred Quinlan, along with the Nicolo Brothers. Sardi would be named to numerous All Star teams while leading Massachusetts in total touchdowns. He would go on to play College Football at Louisiana State University, where he scored on a 94-yard run against Rice University on October 4, 1952.

Saugus followed up their 1949 Championship season by going 8-2 and winning their second consecutive Exchange Bowl, this time a 30-12 victory over Brockton. Richie Nicolo was the star QB again and was helped by Charlie Murphy, Jim Driscoll, Leo Kane, Tony Serino, Charlie Woodell, and Ted Fredericks. This was Saugus’ second consecutive Exchange Bowl championship, marking the end of the Saugus Sachems Football Golden Era.

After the 1950 Exchange Bowl championship, he kept Saugus competitive throughout the 1950s and led the program to conference championships in 1953 and 1959. The 1953 Sachems team was led by Bob Belyea, John Leahy, and Doug MacNeill while the 1959 team was led by David Matthews, Richie Burt, and Jim Kelleher. Other notable players during the 1950s, included Ed Healey, Bob Piwowarski, Dick Rohrbacker, John Naples, Matt Light, William Banks, Vito Russo, and John Matrona.
1961–1972 (Sustaining Competitiveness):
Bernard Stead (1961-1963)
Bernard Stead coached from 1961 to 1963, but the program struggled during his tenure going a combined 1-25. Tom Carr was the only All-Star Stead coached.
Walter Sheridan (1964-1966)

Walter Sheridan took over in 1964 and helped rebuild the team, highlighted by a 7-2 season in 1966. That 1966 team was led by several All Stars including Christie Serino, Eddie McGuire, John Dancewicz, Jim Mancuso, Richie Lombardo, and Don Murray. Serino, with hockey being his best sport, would go on to become a division 1 Head Hockey Coach at Merrimack College followed by a very successful tenure as the head hockey coach at Massachusetts Prep High School Hockey Powerhouse Malden Catholic, cementing his legacy as a champion. Other notable players were All Stars Ronnie Barressi and John Sands, as well as Dick Serino and Harold Kingman.
Paul Maguire (1967-1972)

Paul Maguire coached from 1967 through 1972, with Saugus showing improvement in the late 1960s and early 1970s, including a Northeastern Conference championship in 1969. Notable players during this era were Jim Canole, Lou O'Neil, Bob Osgood, Richie DeSisito, Bill Eichel, Bill Babcock, Richard Conti, John Richards, Dan Heaney and Steve Nelson.
1973–1983: (The Ginolfi Era):
Mike Ginolfi (First tenure 1973-1983)
Mike “Gino” Ginolfi took over as the Sachems head coach in 1973. Coach Ginolfi restored Saugus as a competitive force.

His 1975 Sachems football team was the best Sachems team since the Golden Era. Saugus went 9-1, winning the Northeastern Conference title. Saugus was led by John Nicolo, Doug Mackie, Steve Gannon, Tom Heney, and Pat Sullivan. All were named to numerous All Star Teams.
Gannon went on to play college football at Holy Cross, being one of the program’s greatest players of all time. He is a member of both the Saugus High and Holy Cross Athletic Halls of Fame.

Mackie was named High School All American in 1975 and was considered the top recruit in the United States during his senior season. He would go on to continue his football career at Ohio State and played for the great Woody Hayes. Unfortunately injuries interrupted Mackie’s college career causing him to miss most of his junior and senior seasons. Despite his history of injuries, Mackie did play professionally for the Tampa Bay Bandits and New Jersey Generals of the United States Football League. He was selected as a 1984 Pro Football Newsweekly All-Pro along with his teammate/running back Herschel Walker, as he was part of the starting offensive line who helped Walker set the still standing, single-season, pro football rushing record of 2,411 yards. Mackie also played in the NFL for the Atlanta Falcons and was a member of the New York Giants and New Orleans Saints but did not appear in any games for either team.

Nicolo would go on to play college football at Ithaca College where in 1979 during his senior season, he would go on to be named a Division III All American and helped lead the Ithaca Bombers to a National Championship. Nicolo, who was also an excellent baseball player, led Ithaca’s Baseball team to the 1980 National Championship where he was named MVP. Nicolo would go on to play one year of minor league baseball in 1980 in the New York-Penn League for the Auburn Americans (who were affiliated with the Los Angeles Dodgers and Cleveland Indians). Nicolo would go on to be inducted into the Ithaca College Athletic Hall of Fame as a player in 1986 and twice more with both National Championship Teams. This led to Saugus creating their own Athletic Hall of Fame in 1987, by his father-in-law, Dr. John Mangini, which included the following Sachems Football players in their Inaugural Class: John Nicolo, Sardi Nicolo, Christie Serino, Doug Mackie, George Laskey, Stan Green, John “Iron Mike” Harrington, and Art Spinney.

Saugus took a step back in 1976, however, the Sachems were back on top in 1977 going 9-1 and winning the Northeastern Conference for the second time in three seasons. Coach Ginolfi went on to win numerous Coach of the Year awards following the season. The 1977 squad was led by all stars George Nicolo, Frank Serino, Paul Serino, who was named Boston Globe All Scholastic, Frank Doyle, John Coffee, and Tim Fawcett, who went on to become a very well-known and popular police officer in Saugus.

Saugus followed the 1977 season by going 6-3-1 in 1978 and 5-5 in 1979 to close out the decade. Don Trainor, Bill Peach, Mike Allen, Phil Nigro, along with Steve Peach led Saugus during those seasons. Steve Peach went on to become one of the greatest Quarterbacks to ever play for Saugus. He was the first player to be named a Lynn Item All Star 3 times. Steve would lead Saugus to a 5-5 record in 1980. Steve would go on to play college football at Syracuse. He was offered a scholarship to play at Boston College but turned it down. That scholarship he turned down ended up going to the great Doug Flutie. Peach eventually transferred to Boston College where he was their starting punter in 1984 and 1985. Other Sachems who made All Star teams during the 1979 seasons were Eric Taylor and Gary Quinlan while Bob Cordeau and Arthur Polimeno were all stars from the 1980 team.

The 1981 Sachems season was the worst season for Ginolfi during his first tenure as they went 1-9. Saugus bounced back in 1982 going 5-4-1. That season Saugus was led by Steve Fauci, Anthony Cogliano, Mark Strange, and Anthony Guthro. 1983 Saugus fell back to below .500 going 4-6. The team was led by Tom Trainor, Kevin Pelley, and Bob Cinelli.

Ginolfi would step down after the 1983 season and moved into athletic administration. His coaching tree shaped Saugus football for decades through assistants and former players who followed him into the head coaching role.
1984–1993: Inconsistency and Brief Success
Kevin Ward (1984-1990)

Kevin Ward took over in 1984, and the program went through several down years, though the 1987 team rebounded to go 7-3 and share the Northeastern Conference title. Marc Fauci emerged as one of the Sachems greatest players. He was named Boston Globe All Scholastic in 1989. Fauci would go on to play college football at Boston University (BU). While at BU, Fauci would play Linebacker and was twice named Co-Captain as a junior and senior. Fauci led BU to arguably its best season ever in 1993 when they went 12-1 and finished the regular season with a perfect 11-0 mark, the first unbeaten and untied record in program history. Fauci was named a second-team All-America by The Sports Network and National Weekly Football Gazette and a third-team All-America selection by the Associated Press.
Mike “Bonty” Bontempo (1991-1993)

The 1990 team went 8-2, which was Saugus’s best record in years. After that, Mike “Bonty” Bontempo took over and coached through 1993, but the program struggled during that span going 1-29. During his tenure he coached All Stars Sean Publicover and Joe Attubato.
1994–2004: Rebuilding and Setbacks
Mike Ginolfi (Second Tenure 1994-1995)

Mike Ginolfi returned in 1994 and quickly helped revive the program. After a 0-10 season that year, Saugus broke through in 1995 with a 6-5 record and snapped a 34-game losing streak. Saugus went on to start the season 5-0 and were ranked as high as 16th in the Boston Herald High School football rankings. Saugus would go on to lose star QB Mike Mabee to injury and ended the season 6-5. Despite the disappointing finish, Saugus football was back and competitive. The 1995 team was led by Abate, Mabee, Matt Nazzaro, LJ McKanas, and Derek Bilton.

Coach Ginolfi retired from coaching after the 1995 season. He will always be remembered as one of the greatest football coaches in Sachem history, as he was a 1993 Saugus High Athletic Hall of Fame inductee, but he was also one of the greatest coaches in Massachusetts Football History as he was inducted into the Massachusetts High School Football Coaches Association Hall of Fame in 1992. Coach Ginolfi would remain Athletic Director at Saugus until he retired from that position in 2002
John Fauci (1996-1998)

John Fauci took over for Coach Ginolfi for the 1996 season. Saugus improved from the previous season, going 7-4. The Sachems were led by John Plunkett, Justin Falite, and LJ McKanas. McKanas would be named to numerous All-Star teams as a RB. He would go on to play college football at Northeastern. While at Northeastern McKanas would go on to set numerous rushing records. During his Senior season in 2001 McKanas set records for most carries, 342, rushing yards, 1756, and rushing touchdowns, 14. He gained over 100 yards rushing in nine games and over 200 in three. He averaged 5.1 yards per carry and 159.6 per game as the team posted a 5-6 record. His 242 rushing yards against Massachusetts is second in the Husky record books. He won numerous awards, including All-New England, All-Conference and first-team Hanson All-America. He also received the Harry Agganis Award as the Outstanding Senior Football Player in New England. In 2009 he was inducted into the Northeastern Athletic Hall of Fame. In 2013 McKanas was a contestant on the popular TV Show Survivor. He finished 9th out of 18 contestants. He was the first of two former Sachems to become a contestant on the popular reality show.

Saugus found similar success in 1997 by going 6-4-1. The Sachems were led by Dominic Zammit, Raphael Zammit, Ryan Leahy, Mike Panzini, and Chris McColgan. In 1998 Saugus took a minor step back going 5-6. The Sachems were led by All Stars Raphael Zammit, Leahy, and Panzini. Zammit broke the school record for rushing touchdowns. Zammit was named All State that season. Zammit would go on to play one season for Division I Central Connecticut before transferring to Division III Curry College where he had great success playing for former Patriots legend Steve Nelson. At Curry, Zammit set several single seasons and career rushing records (since broken).
Dean Sacca (1999-2000)

Dean Sacca became head coach in 1999. The 1999 season had a promising start as Saugus started the year 3-3 however Saugus would end the year 3-8. All Star George Lowe, who played almost every skilled position that year, led the team along with Brian Mirasolo. The Sachems continued to struggle in the 2000 season by going 2-8. Coach Sacca stepped down at the end of the season. Ryan Gould was the only All-Star from the 2000 team.
John Nicolo (2001-2004)

John Nicolo took over as the Sachems Head Coach in 2001. Unfortunately, Coach Nicolo’s tenure did not produce the same success as he had during his playing days. The 2001 Sachems went 2-9 and were led by Pat Quinlan, Pat Eaton, and Kyle Sucharewicz. The 2002 Sachems went 1-10 and were led by Sal Nicolo and All-Star Anthony Barbanti. Sal Nicolo would go on to play two seasons of college football for Division III Bridgewater State Bears under Peter Mazzaferro.

The 2003 Sachems were the most competitive Sachems team since the 1998 team, going 3-8. Junior star Running Back, Mike Nicolo, went on to set the then Sachems single game rushing yards record by running for 300 yards against the Salem Witches. Nicolo followed up that legendary game by running for 241 yards against the Beverly Panthers. Nicolo would go on to finish the season rushing for over 1400 yards and 11 touchdowns. He would be named to several All-Star teams along with Barbanti.

The 2004 Sachems were plagued with injuries to their core players and the promising rebuild came to a stop as they finished the season 0-11. Nicolo missed part of the season and played most of the season with an injured knee and shoulder. Despite the injuries Nicolo was still named an All-Star along with teammate Brian Bianchi. Mike Nicolo would go on to play College Football for New England Division III power Curry College however injuries followed him throughout his college career. Nicolo was inducted into the Curry College Athletic Hall of Fame as a member of the 2007 Curry Football Team, which was ranked 19th Nationally and had won 4-consecutive New England Football Conference Championships.
After the 2004 season, Coach Nicolo stepped down as Head Coach and took on the role of Athletic Director.
2005–2016: (The Broderick Era)
Mike Broderick (2005-2016)

Mike Broderick took over in 2005 and brought stability back to the program. Coach Broderick was the first Sachems Head Coach to have not been under the Ginolfi Coaching Tree since the Paul Maguire days.

Coach Broderick’s first two seasons were rebuilding seasons for the Sachems. His 2005 team went 1-10, led by All Star Alex Klimarchuk. In 2006 the Sachems improved to 3-7. Although the record didn’t seem like much, this team was remembered for becoming the first Saugus team to defeat the Sachems Thanksgiving Day rival, the Peabody Tanners, for the first time in 18 seasons. That Sachems team was led by senior All Star, Rodney Lavoie, who went on to be a contestant on the TV Show Survivor in 2015, the second former Sachem to appear on the hit TV Show. Saugus also had a freshman QB by the name of Mike DiChiaria who had a breakout season. DiChiaria would transfer to the prep school BB&N to finish out his High School career, where DiChiaria made the top 10 in Massachusetts state history for career touchdown passes. He would go on to play college football at Cornell.

In 2007 Saugus took a major step forward and had their first winning season since 1997, going 7-3, their best record since 1996. The 2007 team was led by Paul Sullivan and All Stars Tyler Trainor, Mike Dean, and Brett Reid. The 2008 team also went 7-3 and were again led by All Stars Mike Dean and Brett Reid.

From 2009 through 2011, the Sachems fell back to below .500. Although these teams didn’t have as much success, they still had some All-Star players like Shamir Guillaume and AJ Guthro. Guillaume would go on to set the Sachems single season rushing yards record by rushing for 1,678 yards in 2010.

In 2012 the Sachems were above .500 again going 6-5. The Sachems were led by Tom Trainor, CJ Randolph, Nick Benoit, and Ismael Minaya, with Trainor being named an All-Star.  In 2013 Saugus took a step going 3-8 however Jr. QB Justin Winn had a breakout season and was named All Star.

In 2014 the Sachems were once again above .500. Saugus had a breakout game by RB Dan Cacciola, who broke Mike Nicolo’s school record for rushing yards in a single game by rushing for 367 yards in a Week 1 loss against Winthrop. Saugus would go on to finish the season 6-5, their last winning season as of this writing. The team was once again led by All Star QB Winn who was joined as an All Star with Cacciola. Winn would go on to break Raphael Zammit’s rushing touchdown record by scoring 22 rushing touchdowns.

Saugus dropped back below .500 in 2016 and 2016 going 3-9-1 and 1-10. Brendan Grocki and Cam Williamson were both All Stars for those teams. After the 2016 season Coach Broderick stepped down. Coach Broderick ended his 12-season tenure, the third longest after Coach Janusas (14 seasons) and Coach Ginolfi (13 seasons). Coach Broderick will be remembered for building the Sachems first winning teams of the 21st Century.
2017–Present: (Cummings Era)
Anthony Nalen (2017)

Anthony Nalen was hired in 2017, and Saugus improved from the previous season. Ricky Martinez helped lead the Sachems. Unfortunately, due to a controversy during the 2018 off-season, Nalen was removed as head coach.
Mike Mabee (2018)

After Nalen’s departure, former Sachems great and former player under Coach Ginolfi, Mike Mabee, was hired to serve as interim Head Coach. Coach Mabee was able to guide a competitive team to a 4-7 record. The team was led by All-Star Dante McGrane.
Steve Cummings (2019 – Present)
Steve Cummings took over in 2019 and remains the head coach as of today.

The Sachems under Coach Cummings have seen their ups and downs. The Sachems took a step back during the 2019 season when they went 3-8. The team was led by All Star Marvin Jean as well as Kyle Surette, Sal Franco, Christian Correa, and Javier Martinez.
The 2020 Season was interrupted by the Covid-19 Pandemic, but Saugus was still able to play a 7 game schedule during the season, going 2-5.

The next two seasons Saugus went a combined 2-22 (0-11 in 2021 and 2-11 in 2022). Saugus was a young team during those 2 seasons and were in a rebuild. Saugus was led by All Stars Mike MacEacheran and Braden Faiella.

The 2023 Sachems put together the best Sachem team since 2014, going 5-6. Faiella led the team along with All Stars Tommy DeSimmone, Isaiah Rodriguez, and Dylan Clark. Faiella was a 2-time Captain for the Sachems. He was a 2-time Lynn Item All-Scholastic as well as the Lynn Item Defensive Player of the Year during his Senior season. Faiella is currently playing College Football at the Division II level for Saint Anselm, going into his Junior season in 2026.
The 2024 Sachems went 3-8 and were led by All Stars Koby Jette and Cody Munafo.
The 2025 Sachems went 2-9 with Jette being an All-Star for the second consecutive season.
Conclusion

Saugus football has a proud and deeply rooted history. While the program has not reached the heights of its golden era in recent times, it has produced championship caliber teams, conference titles, and many memorable players who excelled at the college and professional levels. More than wins and losses, being a Sachem has always meant pride, tradition, and commitment to the red and white.
